idiom_name: serde internally tagged enum (#[serde(tag = "type")]) deserialized into the canonical enum
implementation_notes: serde makes the wire tag the router: #[serde(tag = "type")] on the canonical enum tells the derive to read the discriminator and dispatch to the matching variant, so serde_json::from_str::<Canonical>(raw) replaces both the translator registry and the type detection for self-describing formats, and downstream code is an exhaustive match the compiler checks. #[serde(other)] gives an explicit forward-compatible catch-all on the representations that support it, which is how unknown tags are accepted deliberately rather than through a generic Value. Formats that do not fit a tagged object still get an explicit impl TryFrom<WireX> for Canonical or a hand-written Deserialize per format - the derive is the convenience, the mapping is still yours - and a tag sniffer in front of the typed decode is the honest route for untagged input.
pitfalls: The internally tagged representation does not compile for tuple variants (a documented derive error), so newtype variants must wrap a struct or map - often forcing a wire newtype around the payload.

#[serde(untagged)] matches variants in declaration order and reports only the last failure, so a permissive first variant swallows everything and the error names the wrong format; order and specificity are part of the contract.

f64 is the default for JSON numbers: 64-bit ids and money lose precision unless the canonical type uses strings or the arbitrary_precision feature, and serde_json::Value in the canonical model moves the type check to run time.
Borrowed &str fields in a canonical enum tie the message to the input buffer's lifetime; own the canonical message (String) or keep it borrowed strictly inside the parse scope.
